summary: Provides state machine tables for LDP processing on ATM switch label switching routers. The LDP specification had no state machine, and a common one helps different LDP and CR-LDP implementations work together. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A board game needs rules about what happens after each move. This writes those rules for a network protocol so every maker plays the same way.

questions: what is the ldp state machine
what states does an ldp lsp have
what is vc merge in mpls
what is downstream on demand label distribution
subtitle: State tables that say exactly how an ATM switch reacts to each LDP message while building label switched paths.

tldr.problem: The LDP specification has no state machine for processing LDP messages, so different LDP and CR-LDP implementations could handle the same message differently.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines control blocks, states, events and actions as tables for ATM switch LSRs: one set for LSRs without VC-merge, one for LSRs with VC-merge (both downstream-on-demand), and one for downstream unsolicited mode.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document meant to clarify the LDP specification, not to override it. It targets ATM switch LSRs but says the tables can be adapted to other types of LSRs.

today: RFC 3215 is Informational and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It says it clarifies the LDP specification (RFC 3036) without overriding it.

sections.title: Why LDP Needs a State Machine
sections.content:
The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) lets routers set up label switched paths (LSPs). The LDP specification, RFC 3036, does not define a state machine for processing LDP messages. The authors argue that a common one is important for interoperability between different LDP and CR-LDP implementations.

This memo gives state machine tables for ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) switch LSRs. It covers the machinery used to establish and maintain LSPs. It does not describe the separate "LDP controller" that handles session initialization, address mapping messages and the routing interface.

The six message names used throughout are LDP-REQUEST, LDP-MAPPING, LDP-WITHDRAW, LDP-RELEASE, LDP-ABORT (aborts an LSP setup) and LDP-NAK (a notification that rejects a message).
sections.eli5: Two toy makers might build the same robot but make it react differently to the same button. This memo says what the robot must do for every button.

sections.title: Control Blocks, States and Events
sections.content:
Each description uses control blocks, states, events, response actions and state transitions. A control block holds what an LSR needs to handle events for one LSP. For a non-VC-merge LSR, an LSP Control Block is created when a new LDP-REQUEST arrives and deleted when that LSP is torn down. It holds items such as the upstream and downstream label request IDs, the upstream and downstream LDP identifiers, the state, the FEC, and the upstream and downstream labels.

A second kind, the Next Hop Trigger Control Block, handles switching to a better next hop. It uses a timer so the switch happens after a routing transient has had time to stabilize.

The LSP Control Block has four states: IDLE, RESPONSE_AWAITED, ESTABLISHED and RELEASE_AWAITED. Its events include LDP Request, LDP Mapping, LDP Release, LDP Withdraw, LDP Upstream Abort, LDP Downstream NAK, Upstream Lost, Downstream Lost, and internal events such as Internal SetUp, Internal Destroy, Internal Cross-Connect and Internal New NH.
sections.eli5: Each path gets its own index card that records where it is in the process. Each new message tells you how to update the card.

sections.title: Downstream-on-Demand, No VC-Merge
sections.content:
For ATM LSRs without VC-merge capability, downstream-on-demand mode is required, and so is conservative label retention. The tables cover both independent and ordered LSP control.

In IDLE, an LDP Request makes the LSR act in one of two ways. If it is the egress or proxy egress, it picks an upstream label and sends LDP-MAPPING upstream, going to ESTABLISHED. Otherwise it forwards a new LDP-REQUEST toward the next hop and goes to RESPONSE_AWAITED. If it cannot process the request, it sends an LDP-NAK and deletes the control block.

In RESPONSE_AWAITED, an LDP Mapping connects the upstream label to the downstream label and moves the LSP to ESTABLISHED. An abort, an upstream loss or an internal destroy leads to an LDP-ABORT downstream and a return to IDLE. In ESTABLISHED, an LDP Release frees the labels and resources and goes back to IDLE. Events that should never occur in a state are simply ignored as internal implementation errors.
sections.eli5: Passing a note down a line of kids: you ask the next kid, wait for the answer, and once the answer comes back you tell the kid behind you.

sections.title: Next Hop Changes and VC-Merge
sections.content:
When a topology change gives an LSR a better next hop, it may try a "local repair": extend the LSP through the new next hop, release the old path and splice into the new one. If the LSP was created with the "pinned" option (CR-LDP), the LSR ignores the change. The Next Hop Trigger Control Block has the states IDLE, NEW_NH_RETRY and NEW_NH_RESPONSE_AWAITED.

A VC-merge capable LSR can map multiple incoming labels (VPI/VCI) into one outgoing label, possibly only a limited number. For these LSRs the memo uses three kinds of control blocks: Upstream LSP Control Blocks (one per LDP-REQUEST received), Downstream LSP Control Blocks (one per unique LDP-REQUEST sent downstream) and Next Hop Trigger Control Blocks. A Downstream block keeps pointers to the upstream blocks merged into it. Downstream-on-demand is recommended when an upstream LSR has limited merging capability.
sections.eli5: If a road closes, you build a new road and then switch over. Merging is several small streams pouring into one river.

sections.title: Downstream Unsolicited Mode
sections.content:
In downstream unsolicited mode, labels are offered without being requested. The memo considers only ordered LSP control here, because independent control uses liberal label retention and is considered to burn too many ATM resources. Multiple paths are not supported in this version and are left for further study, since multiple next hops with this mode make loops easy to create.

Each FEC has one Downstream LSP Control Block, and a list of Upstream LSP Control Blocks, one per LDP peer. The upstream block has four states: IDLE, ESTABLISHED, RELEASE_AWAITED and RESOURCES_AWAITED. The last one means the LSR is waiting for a local resource such as a label. Events include Internal Downstream Mapping, LDP Release, Internal Withdraw, Resource Available, Delete FEC and Upstream Lost.
sections.eli5: Here the next kid hands you a ticket without being asked. You hand out your own tickets to the kids behind you, and if you run out of tickets you wait.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The state machines are meant to clarify procedures in the LDP specification, not to supplant or override them. An implementation may be vulnerable to spurious events from an external source. Events are either internal events or external events caused by receiving an LDP message.

LDP messages may be protected using the mechanisms in the LDP specification. Security considerations about spurious internal events are not addressed in this document.
sections.eli5: A rulebook cannot stop someone shouting fake moves. Protection comes from the main LDP rules, and this memo does not cover fake moves made inside the machine.
